'''John Dennis Biggers''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|ɪ|g|ər|s}}; 1923 – April 7, 2018) was a British and American [[Reproductive biology|reproductive biologist]] and [[Reproductive endocrinology and infertility|reproductive physiologist]] who helped pioneer [[in vitro fertilisation]]. He played a founding role in the scientific study of reproductive physiology, won many scientific awards for developing technology which would become central to human IVF, and engaged in public outreach regarding the ethics of artificial fertilisation.

== Early life and education ==
Biggers was born in 1923 in [[Reading, Berkshire]], to Wilfred Norman Biggers, a chemistry and physics teacher, and Winnifred Gardner, a [[British Airways]] employee.<ref name=marquard2018>{{cite news |last= Marquard|first= Bryan|date= 2018-05-05|title= John Biggers, 94, pioneer researcher for in vitro fertilization|url= https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2018/05/05/john-biggers-pioneer-researcher-for-vitro-fertilization-dies/mdUlfC565x5KOxb3gBzSRO/story.html|work= Boston Globe|location= Boston, MA|access-date= 2018-08-06}}</ref> Biggers studied veterinary science at the [[Royal Veterinary College]]. He subsequently shifted his focus to mammalian physiology, in which he earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the [[University of London]].<ref name=currentobituary />

==Development of IVF==
After completing his graduate education, Biggers first worked at the [[University of Sydney]], then in 1955 moved to [[St John's College, Cambridge]] under a [[Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan|commonwealth fellowship]], and from there became a senior lecturer at the Royal Veterinary College.<ref name="currentobituary">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title= John D. Biggers Obituary|url= https://www.currentobituary.com/obit/219582|work= Current Obituary|date= 2018-04-07|access-date= 2018-08-06}}</ref> While lecturing at University College London in 1958, he coauthored a landmark [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] paper with Dame [[Anne McLaren]], which for the first time reported the successful development and birth of [[Laboratory mouse|mice]] cultivated in vitro. Professor Henry Leese of [[Hull York Medical School]], writing for the [[Reproduction (journal)|Society for Reproduction and Fertility]], labelled this "one of the most significant papers in the history of reproductive biology and medicine", and this development is widely considered a crucial milestone towards in vitro fertilisation in humans.<ref name="marquard2018">{{cite news |last= Marquard|first= Bryan|date= 2018-05-05|title= John Biggers, 94, pioneer researcher for in vitro fertilization|url= https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2018/05/05/john-biggers-pioneer-researcher-for-vitro-fertilization-dies/mdUlfC565x5KOxb3gBzSRO/story.html|work= Boston Globe|location= Boston, MA|access-date= 2018-08-06}}</ref><ref name=stfobituary>{{cite news |last=Leese |first=Henry |title= In Memoriam Professor John Biggers |url= http://srf-reproduction.org/who-we-are/in-memoriam/|work= Society for Reproduction and Fertility|date= 2018-04-07|access-date= 2018-08-06}}</ref><ref name=albertini2013>{{cite journal |last1=Albertini |first1=David |last2=McGinnis |first2=Lynda |year=2013 |title=A catalyst for change in reproductive science: John D. Biggers as a mentor's mentor |journal=Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics |volume=30 |issue=8 |pages=979–994 |doi=10.1007/s10815-013-0096-9 |pmid=24077825 |pmc=3790115 }}</ref><ref name=summers2014>{{cite journal |last1= Summers|first1= Michael |date=2015-11-05 |title= Reflections of one man's life in Nature: Professor John D Biggers, DSc, PhD|url= https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263294380|journal= Human Fertility|volume= 17|issue= S1|pages= 2–6|doi= 10.3109/14647273.2014.919181|pmid= 24939344 |s2cid= 7081190 |access-date= 2018-08-06}}</ref>

Biggers moved to the United States in 1959, working first at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], moving to [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1967, and finally becoming a professor at the [[Harvard Medical School]] in 1972. During this time, he worked on problems in [[embryo culture]], [[embryo transfer]], [[cryobiology]], sperm preservation, and [[Biostatistics|the statistics of experimental design]].<ref name=summers2014 /> Biggers was a founding member and president of the Society for the Study of Reproduction, won several awards for his research from organizations like the [[Bedford Stem Cell Research Foundation]], and authored more than 250 scientific papers.<ref name= marquard2018/> In addition to experimentation and mentoring, Biggers engaged publicly in ethical and policy advocacy regarding IVF technology. [[Howard W. Jones]] credited Biggers with providing critical support for the initiation of clinical IVF in the United States, which led to [[Elizabeth Jordan Carr|the first American baby]] being born by means of IVF.<ref name= albertini2013/> Biggers was regularly interviewed in the popular press on issues of reproductive ethics.<ref name= albertini2013/>

== Notable Awards ==
John Biggers received many awards and honors, the most notable being the Marshall Medal from the Society for the Study of Reproduction and the Pioneer Award from the International Embryo Technology Society.<ref>{{Cite web |title=John D. Biggers: School of Medicine |url=https://almanac.upenn.edu/articles/john-d.-biggers-school-of-medicine |access-date=2026-02-22 |website=almanac.upenn.edu |language=en}}</ref>
